Recruitment in FINN: the options and how to choose them

Source: R/recruitment-doc.R
recruitment.Rd

Recruitment in FINN is set in several places: the regeneration process function and its arguments in createProcess() (or createHybrid()), two arguments of finn(), and the likelihood and recruitment mode of fit(), predict.finn_class() and simulateForest(). This page says what each option does, how they act together, and which combination to use for which purpose. The individual help pages carry the full argument descriptions.

One simulated year of recruitment runs in three steps. The regeneration process returns an EXPECTED recruitment per hectare for every site, patch and species. This rate is turned into a whole number of recruits per patch, which enter the stand as new cohorts at finn(recruits_dbh = ). During fit() the expected rate (not the drawn recruits), summed over an observation interval, is compared with the observed reg by the regeneration likelihood.

The recruitment process

The process is the func of the regeneration process passed to finn(regeneration_process = ). All mechanistic variants share the same core: a light response gated by the species parameter parReg, times the environmental response exp(env), plus the additive floor createProcess(reg_floor = ) of the regeneration process (default 1e-3 stems per ha and year).

  • regeneration(): the core alone. The expected recruitment is not bounded; it grows with the environmental response.

  • regeneration_capped(): the default since 0.2.0, used when regeneration_process is NULL. The core is capped by a Beverton-Holt term, K m / (K + m). createProcess(cap = "all") (default) gives one cap K shared by all species, cap = "species" one per species. The cap carries a prior, prior_lambda * (log K - log prior)^2, with prior = "max_obs_recruits" (the largest observed recruitment per ha and year) and prior_lambda = 0.1 by default. The cap bounds the MEAN recruitment only. It does not bound the variance of the recruit draw, which around a capped mean is still K + K^2 / theta (see the dispersion section below).

  • regeneration_saturation(): the same function as regeneration_capped() under its older name, kept as a deprecated alias for one release.

  • regeneration_adult(): the capped process with a seed source. The recruitment of a species is multiplied by f(A) = A / (A + A_half), where A is the density of its own adults (stems above an adult threshold x) pooled over the patches of the site. A species without adults on a site recruits only at reg_floor. x and A_half are declared through createProcess(custom_parameters = ); see its help page.

  • regeneration_adult_effect(): the adult density as an effect on recruitment instead of a gate, f(A) = f0 + (1 - f0) A / (A + A_half) with f0 = plogis(reg_adult_logitf0), the share of the potential recruitment a species gets without adults on the site (seed rain from outside, advance regeneration). Prefer it to regeneration_adult() whenever a species must be able to establish where it has no adults: colonisation from an empty stand, and any free run from bare ground, need f0 > 0. f0 -> 1 removes the adult effect, f0 -> 0 is regeneration_adult().

A regeneration process built with createHybrid() replaces the whole equation by a network. In 0.2.0 it has no Beverton-Holt cap: createHybrid() accepts cap, prior and prior_lambda, but the network does not use them.

From expected recruitment to recruits

The expected rate per ha times patch_size (in ha) is the expected number of recruits per patch. createProcess(sample_regeneration = ) decides how it becomes a whole number:

  • sample_regeneration = TRUE (default): recruits are drawn from a negative binomial with that mean and size theta (the dispersion, next section), using createProcess(regeneration_sampler = ). "refined" (default since 0.2.0) draws the Gamma-mixed Poisson exactly where its rate is below 2 and uses a Gaussian approximation above. "gaussian" reproduces results published before 0.2.0; its guards act as a recruitment floor of 0.0011 per cell and year (see rnbinom_torch_refined()).

  • sample_regeneration = FALSE: the expected number is used and rounded. Wherever the expected number per patch is below 0.5 the rounding delivers no recruit at all. At small patches and low rates this is a silent zero for every sparse species, however well its rate is calibrated.

The recruit dispersion theta

par_theta_recruits is the negative-binomial size theta, one value per species. It sets the variance of the recruit draw, mu + mu^2 / theta, and the width of the negative-binomial regeneration likelihood. Three arguments of createProcess() (and createHybrid()) control it:

  • dispersion_parameter: the starting value, or the fixed value when theta is not trained. Default 1.

  • optimizeTheta: TRUE (default) trains theta. FALSE keeps it at dispersion_parameter for the whole fit, in the draw and in the likelihood alike.

  • theta_floor: a lower bound applied wherever theta is read, trained or not. Default 0.5 since 0.2.0; 0 or NULL removes it. A fixed dispersion_parameter below the floor is raised to the floor.

With the default fit(rb_gradient = TRUE), theta is set only by the regeneration likelihood. On sparse, zero-heavy recruitment data the likelihood optimum of theta is very small: a small theta widens the likelihood and so lowers the loss without improving the predicted mean, and the same small theta makes the simulated draws bursty. A free theta can therefore run away.

What the floor does: it keeps the fit stable, and in a fit run to convergence it costs nothing we could resolve. In one converged pair of fits on the German national forest inventory (2000 epochs, about 126 000 optimizer steps), the model with the floor predicted the recruitment level on a spatially blocked holdout at 1.06 times the observed and the one with a fixed theta of 1 (optimizeTheta = FALSE) at 1.04; their recruitment likelihoods were within 0.003 of each other (0.897 and 0.894 relative to an intercept-only null), and they agreed on basal area, stem numbers, growth and the mortality AUC to three decimals. Early in a fit the two settings differ: after 50 of those 2000 epochs (3 150 optimizer steps on that inventory) a floored theta still put the level about 12 times too high, a fixed theta 2 to 3 times, and a free theta had run away by four orders of magnitude. Count the budget in optimizer steps, not epochs: on a small data set 50 epochs can be 50 steps. So read the recruitment level only once the parameters have settled ($param_history), whichever setting you use; for short fits, a fixed theta gets the level right sooner.

The likelihood and the observation operator

fit(loss_family = c(regeneration = )) chooses the regeneration likelihood. "nbinom" (default) uses theta as above. "poisson" has no dispersion parameter and so cannot collapse; theta then only shapes the recruit draw.

finn(recruit_obs_weight = w) is an observation operator: it maps the predicted and the observed recruitment per ha alike into the count space of the sampling design before they are compared, so that the likelihood sees the counts that were actually tallied. For an angle-count inventory w = g(recruits_dbh) / BAF. For a fixed-radius small-tree plot that counts the stems in a diameter band below the recruitment threshold,

w = plot area (ha) x residence time in the band (years) / observation period (years),

where the residence time is the band width divided by the diameter growth of the stems in it. One tallied stem then stands for 1 / w recruits per ha over the observation period. The residence time is an assumption and should be estimated from the data where possible: w scales every absolute recruitment number the fit returns, though not the ranking between model configurations.

In 0.2.0 recruit_obs_weight is applied only under "nbinom". With loss_family["regeneration"] = "poisson" (or "mse", "gaussian") the term scores the per-ha values as they are and recruit_obs_weight has no effect, without a warning; the Poisson variance then is that of a per-ha value, not of the tallied count. The Poisson term adds fit(trees_offset = ) (default 0.01) to the prediction.

Feeding observed recruitment

fit(loss_recruit = "observed") drives the simulated stand with the observed recruitment instead of the regeneration process. The observed reg divided by period_length is the expected recruitment per ha and year in every year of that interval; times patch_size it is drawn per patch by the recruit sampler, as above. Growth, mortality and competition run and are trained as usual. The regeneration term is weighted 0 and every regeneration parameter (species parameters, environment response, cap, theta, custom parameters) is frozen for that call. predict() and simulateForest() take recruits = "observed" and the table obs_recruits to simulate the same way. With observed recruitment the model is not an autonomous simulator: every simulated year must lie in an observed interval, and bare-ground, succession or projection runs are refused.

The intended use is a staged calibration when the inventory samples small trees too sparsely to calibrate recruitment jointly with the rest. First fit the demography (growth, mortality, competition) with fit(loss_recruit = "observed"); then fit the regeneration process on its own, with the other processes frozen (optimizeSpecies/optimizeEnv = FALSE, or through loss_weights).

One caveat: the fed per-site count is a noisy estimate, and it is re-sampled as if it were the mean. The observation noise of a sparse small-tree count therefore enters the simulated stand. On the German national forest inventory one tallied small tree stands for about 1 600 stems per ha per decade, and the fed counts carry a variance comparable to that of the whole stem-count column, which costs accuracy in the simulated stem counts.

Choosing

  • Default settings (regeneration_capped, trained theta with theta_floor = 0.5, "nbinom"): the fit is stable, and in one converged pair of fits on the German national forest inventory the recruitment level was calibrated as well as with a fixed theta. Do not read the level from a fit stopped early; check that $param_history has settled.

  • For short fits, or when the recruitment level should not depend on how long the fit runs: keep theta fixed (createProcess(optimizeTheta = FALSE), with dispersion_parameter 1 or higher), or use fit(loss_family = c(..., regeneration = "poisson")). Mind that recruit_obs_weight is ignored under "poisson" (above).

  • When small trees are sampled too sparsely, and in particular when the spatial pattern of recruitment is not predictable from the predictors (on the German national forest inventory no configuration ranked sites better than a Spearman correlation of about 0.08 out of sample): use the staged route of the previous section.

  • Check before interpreting recruitment: compare the predicted and the observed total recruitment, and the regeneration loss in m$history against its intercept-only baseline (with loss_weights = "auto", a value of 1 is no better than predicting the mean).

See also

createProcess(), createHybrid(), finn(), fit(), simulateForest(), regeneration(), regeneration_capped(), regeneration_adult(), regeneration_adult_effect()

Examples

library(data.table)
# three sites of the bundled Oregon FIA sample and two epochs per fit, to
# show the options; a real calibration uses all sites and many epochs
sites <- 1:3
Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species)
obs   <- fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites]
env   <- fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites]
init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp)

# the default regeneration process: a cap shared by all species with its
# prior from the data, and a trained recruit dispersion with a floor of 0.5
FINN.seed(1)
m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
          growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),
          mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),
          regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped))
fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,
    patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%
exp(as.numeric(m$reg_logK))         # the cap, recruits per ha and year
#> [1] 1.633672
max(obs$reg / obs$period_length)    # its prior: the largest observed rate
#> [1] 1.666667

# a fixed recruit dispersion and no recruitment floor
m_fixed <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
                growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),
                mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),
                regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped,
                                                     optimizeTheta = FALSE,
                                                     dispersion_parameter = 1,
                                                     reg_floor = 0))

# the first stage of a staged calibration: the observed recruits drive the
# stand, the regeneration process is frozen and its loss term is dropped
fit(m_fixed, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,
    patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE, loss_recruit = "observed")
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=20%, ba=20%, trees=20%, growth=20%, mortality=20%
#> ℹ recruits = "observed": 6 site-year(s) after a site's last census get no recruits; nothing after a site's last census enters the objective.
#> ℹ recruits = "observed": the observed recruitment drives the stand; 2 regeneration parameter tensor(s) frozen and the regeneration term weighted 0 in this call
do.call(rbind, m_fixed$history)     # the regeneration column (6) is 0
#>          [,1]      [,2]      [,3]     [,4]     [,5] [,6] [,7]
#> [1,] 1.117239 0.7862722 0.3301393 24.33878 1.379735    0    0
#> [2,] 1.777334 0.7268226 0.3588108 25.82573 1.354413    0    0
